avenues.title: Vote in an election
avenues.one_liner: Decide who holds the offices that run your city, your ward and your block.
avenues.what_it_is: An election is a fixed window in which residents choose who holds public office. Most of it is not the voting itself — it is the paperwork and the dates around it: being registered, knowing what is on your ballot, knowing where and when you can hand it in. That is the part that is technically public and practically invisible.
avenues.why_it_matters: Offices decided at an election set budgets, write rules, and appoint the people who enforce them. Every other avenue on this site leads to a body that someone was elected to, or appointed by someone who was.
avenues.local_note: Every registered voter in the District is mailed a ballot. You can post it back, put it in any drop box, vote early, or vote on election day — and because the District runs vote centers rather than assigned polling places, **you may use any vote center in the city, whichever one suits your day.** Your address still decides what is on your ballot, and your precinct still decides how your results are reported.

opportunities.title: 2026 General Election
opportunities.summary: DC votes on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Every registered voter is mailed a ballot; you can return it by mail or drop box, vote early from October 26, or vote on the day at any vote center in the District.

window.note: Set by law as the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November of each even-numbered year.

sub_windows.label: Ballots start going out in the post
sub_windows.note: Every registered voter in the District is mailed a ballot without asking for one. DCBOE marks this start date tentative on its own calendar. If yours has not arrived a couple of weeks after it, that is worth chasing rather than waiting.

sub_windows.label: Last day to register or update your registration by mail or online
sub_windows.note: This is the deadline for applications and updates received by mail or online. Missing it does not stop you voting: you can still register in person at an Early Vote Center from October 26, or at any vote center on election day, and cast a full ballot the same visit.

sub_windows.label: Last day to request a mail ballot
sub_windows.note: For voters who need to request one — for example to have it sent to a different address. Most registered DC voters do not need to do anything: a ballot is mailed to them.

sub_windows.label: Last day for military and overseas voters to request a ballot
sub_windows.note: A later deadline, and it applies only to voters covered by the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act — District voters serving in the military or living abroad. If that is you, the October 19 date above is not yours.

sub_windows.label: Mail ballot drop boxes are open
sub_windows.note: DCBOE lists this period as tentative on its own calendar. The last collection is at 8:00 p.m. on election day.

sub_windows.label: Early voting
sub_windows.note: Early Vote Centers are open every day in this period from 8:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. You can register and vote in the same visit.

sub_windows.label: Election day
sub_windows.note: You can register and cast a full ballot in person at a vote center on the day. All voters who are in line at 8:00 p.m. may cast a ballot.

sub_windows.label: Post your ballot back
sub_windows.note: A mailed ballot must be postmarked on or before election day — not received by. DCBOE accepts postmarked ballots that arrive up to Friday, November 13.

sub_windows.label: Last day to prove you were eligible, if you cast a special ballot
sub_windows.note: A special ballot is one you are given when your eligibility cannot be confirmed at the vote center. It is set aside rather than counted, and it only counts if you follow up by this date.

sub_windows.label: Last day to fix a problem with your mail ballot
sub_windows.note: If your mail ballot is rejected — most often because the signature does not match the one on file — you can correct it up to this date and it will be counted. Nobody tells you automatically. DCBOE runs a toll-free line and a website where you can check whether your ballot was counted, and why if it was not.

avenues.title: Comment on a proposed rule
avenues.one_liner: When an agency wants to change the rules, there is a window where it has to read what you write.
avenues.what_it_is: Agencies cannot usually change a regulation quietly. They publish the proposed text and open a comment period — normally 30 days — during which anyone can write in. The comments become part of the record the agency has to respond to. Almost nobody uses this, which is exactly why a single well-argued comment carries weight here that it does not carry anywhere else.
avenues.why_it_matters: Regulations are where a law becomes the thing that actually happens to you. The comment period is the only routine moment a resident is invited into that text before it binds them.
avenues.local_note: DC publishes the Register twice a month. The comment window is inside the notice, not on a calendar anywhere — which is precisely the fine print this project exists to surface.

avenues.title: Say something about the budget
avenues.one_liner: Once a year the people who set the budget have to sit and listen to residents, on the record.
avenues.what_it_is: Budget and oversight hearings are scheduled, public, and open to anyone who signs up in time. You get a few minutes on the record, and staff read the written version whether or not you speak. It is the most concrete point of contact between a resident and a number in a spreadsheet.
avenues.why_it_matters: A budget is the only document that says what a government will actually do next year. Everything else is intention.
avenues.local_note: The Council holds performance and budget oversight hearings each spring, one per agency. Signing up to testify is a short form and a deadline, and it is the least-known door in DC government.

avenues.title: Report something broken
avenues.one_liner: The pothole, the streetlight, the pile that has been there three weeks — reporting it creates a record with a number on it.
avenues.what_it_is: A service request is the smallest unit of civic participation, and the only one most people ever use. What is not obvious is that each report becomes a tracked, public record — which means a street with twenty logged reports is a street that can be pointed at in a hearing.
avenues.why_it_matters: Individually it fixes a thing. Collectively it is evidence, and evidence is what the other avenues on this site run on.
avenues.local_note: DC’s 311 record is public, which is what makes the second step — keep the number — worth saying out loud.
